subject: electrical engineering
title: Kirchhoff's laws
text: Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed loop in a circuit is zero. It follows from conservation of energy: a charge that travels around a loop returns to its starting potential. Kirchhoff's current law states that the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it, which follows from conservation of charge. Together with Ohm's law, V = IR, the two laws allow the current in every branch of a linear circuit to be found. In mesh analysis, a loop current is assigned to each independent loop and the voltage law is written for each loop; in nodal analysis, node voltages are the unknowns and the current law is written at each node.

subject: civil engineering
title: Bending stress in beams
text: For a beam in bending, the normal stress at a distance y from the neutral axis is σ = My/I, where M is the bending moment at the section and I is the second moment of area of the cross-section about the neutral axis. The stress is zero at the neutral axis and greatest at the outer fibres, where y equals the distance c to the extreme fibre. The section modulus Z = I/c therefore gives the maximum stress directly as σmax = M/Z. A simply supported beam of span L carrying a uniformly distributed load w has its maximum bending moment at midspan, equal to wL²/8. Deflection is limited in design as well as stress; a common serviceability limit for floor beams is span/360.

subject: computer engineering
title: TCP connection management
text: TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake. The client sends a SYN segment carrying its initial sequence number. The server replies with a SYN-ACK segment that acknowledges the client's sequence number and carries the server's own initial sequence number. The client then sends an ACK acknowledging the server's sequence number, and the connection is established. Closing a connection normally takes four segments, because each direction is shut down independently with a FIN and an ACK. A host that performs an active close waits in the TIME_WAIT state for twice the maximum segment lifetime before releasing the connection.

subject: mechanical engineering
title: Heat engines and the Carnot limit
text: A heat engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, converts part of it to work, and rejects the rest to a cold reservoir. Its thermal efficiency is the work output divided by the heat input. The Carnot cycle, made of two isothermal and two adiabatic reversible processes, sets the upper limit: η = 1 − Tc/Th, with both temperatures in kelvin. An engine operating between 600 K and 300 K can therefore convert at most half of its heat input into work. Real engines fall short of this limit because of friction, heat loss and irreversible processes.

subject: architecture
title: The classical orders
text: The Doric order has a plain cushion-shaped capital and its columns stand directly on the floor without a base. The Ionic order has a capital with a pair of volutes, or scrolls, and its columns stand on a base. The Corinthian order has an ornate capital carved with acanthus leaves and also stands on a base. The Doric column is the stoutest of the three, with a height of about seven times its diameter, while the Corinthian is the most slender. The Parthenon in Athens is the best-known Doric temple.

subject: architecture
title: Passive solar design
text: Passive solar design heats and cools a building through its form and materials rather than mechanical systems. In the northern hemisphere, the main glazing faces south so that low winter sun enters the building, while roof overhangs sized for the latitude shade the same windows from the high summer sun. Thermal mass such as concrete floors or masonry walls absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, smoothing temperature swings. Cross-ventilation, created by openings on opposite sides of a room, removes heat in summer. Insulation and airtightness keep the collected heat from escaping.

subject: architecture
title: Gothic structure
text: Gothic cathedrals achieved tall, thin walls and large windows by concentrating the loads of the stone vault onto a few points. Pointed arches direct thrust more steeply downward than round arches, reducing the outward push on the walls. Ribbed vaults channel the weight of the ceiling along ribs to piers. Flying buttresses, external half-arches, carry the remaining outward thrust from the upper walls across the side aisles to massive buttress piers. Pinnacles placed on top of the buttress piers add weight that helps turn the thrust downward into the foundations. Because the walls no longer carried the main loads, they could be opened up for stained glass.

subject: medicine
title: The cardiac cycle
text: The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in one heartbeat. It begins with atrial systole, when the atria contract and push the last of the blood into the ventricles. Ventricular systole follows: pressure in the ventricles rises, the atrioventricular valves close, producing the first heart sound, and once ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected. In diastole the ventricles relax; the semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound, and the atrioventricular valves open so the ventricles refill. At a resting heart rate of 75 beats per minute, one cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds.

subject: medicine
title: Blood glucose regulation
text: Blood glucose is kept within a narrow range by two pancreatic hormones. When glucose rises after a meal, beta cells in the islets of Langerhans release insulin. Insulin increases glucose uptake by muscle and fat cells and stimulates the liver to store glucose as glycogen, lowering blood glucose. When glucose falls, alpha cells release glucagon, which stimulates the liver to break glycogen down and to make new glucose by gluconeogenesis. This is an example of negative feedback. In type 1 diabetes the beta cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process, so insulin must be given; in type 2 diabetes the tissues become resistant to insulin.

subject: pharmacology
title: Pharmacokinetics
text: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug, summarised as absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Absorption is the movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream; intravenous drugs have a bioavailability of 100 percent. Distribution is the spread of the drug into tissues. Metabolism, mostly in the liver, converts the drug into metabolites that are usually more water-soluble. Excretion, mostly by the kidneys, removes it. The elimination half-life is the time taken for plasma concentration to fall by half. After about five half-lives a drug is considered almost entirely eliminated, and with repeated dosing it takes about the same time to reach steady state.

subject: medicine
title: Wound healing
text: Wound healing proceeds through four overlapping stages. In haemostasis, blood vessels constrict and platelets form a clot that stops bleeding. In inflammation, neutrophils and then macrophages enter the wound and clear bacteria and debris. In proliferation, fibroblasts lay down granulation tissue, new blood vessels form, and the wound edges contract. In remodelling, which can last a year or more, collagen is reorganised and the scar gains strength, although it never regains the full strength of unwounded skin.

subject: biology
title: Photosynthesis
text: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts in two linked stages. In the light-dependent reactions, on the thylakoid membranes, light energy splits water, releasing oxygen, and the energy is stored in ATP and NADPH. In the light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, in the stroma, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, and ATP and NADPH from the first stage are used to reduce the products to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, from which glucose is built. Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature each limit the rate when in short supply.

subject: history of medicine
title: The discovery of penicillin
text: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould, Penicillium notatum, killed bacteria on a culture plate. The substance was hard to isolate, and little followed until 1940, when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford purified penicillin and showed that it protected infected mice. The first human patient was treated in 1941. Mass production in the United States during the Second World War made penicillin widely available by 1944, and Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945.
